items.context: The spec has no scope set. User management could be a new standalone scenario, an extension of scenario-authenticator, or features added to web-console. The authenticator already has user CRUD, sessions, RBAC, OAuth, 2FA, and CLI user commands. Recommendation: Option B — extend scenario-authenticator, since it already owns the user data model and has the infrastructure.

options.label: New standalone scenario (scenarios/user-management/)
options.rationale: Clean separation of concerns. Auth stays focused on identity verification; user-mgmt handles profiles, lifecycle, admin. More complex to integrate but cleaner boundaries.

options.label: Extend scenario-authenticator
options.rationale: Builds on existing user table, auth middleware, and CLI. Avoids data sync issues. Risk: authenticator scope grows large. Most pragmatic path since auth already owns users.

options.label: Add user management views to web-console only
options.rationale: Minimal new backend — just API endpoints in web-console calling authenticator APIs. Limited to admin-facing features, no self-service.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: User management is broad. We need to define what's in v1 vs deferred. The authenticator already covers registration, login, password reset, RBAC, OAuth, 2FA, API keys, and basic audit logging. Recommendation: Option B — profiles + admin + self-service as a focused but complete package.

options.label: Profiles only (display name, avatar, preferences, metadata)
options.rationale: Smallest scope. Quick to ship. Other scenarios can start consuming profile data immediately. Leaves admin and self-service for later.

options.label: Profiles + admin dashboard + self-service account management
options.rationale: Complete user management experience. Admin can search/suspend/delete users. Users can edit profile, manage sessions, view login history. More work but delivers full value.

options.label: Full suite including cross-scenario identity federation
options.rationale: Maximum scope: profiles, admin, self-service, plus a shared identity API that any scenario can query for user data. Highest value but most complex and longest timeline.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: The authenticator stores minimal user data (email, hashed password, roles, 2FA secrets). Richer profiles need a schema decision. Recommendation: Option A — separate profiles table is cleanest and avoids bloating the auth users table.

options.label: Separate user_profiles table (FK to auth users)
options.rationale: Clean separation. Auth table stays lean. Profile data can evolve independently. Easy to query join. Standard pattern.

options.label: Extend existing users table with profile columns
options.rationale: Simpler schema, fewer joins. But couples profile changes to auth table migrations. Gets unwieldy as profile fields grow.

options.label: JSON/JSONB column on users table for flexible profile data
options.rationale: Maximum flexibility, no migrations for new fields. But harder to query, index, and validate. Good for unstructured metadata.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: If admin features are included, we need to decide where the UI lives. The web-console already has a React admin interface. Scenario-authenticator has its own UI. Recommendation: Option A — web-console is the natural home for admin tools.

options.label: Add user management pages to web-console UI
options.rationale: Web-console is already the admin hub. Consistent UX. Avoids another UI to maintain. Calls user-mgmt API endpoints.

options.label: Build admin UI within the user-mgmt/authenticator scenario
options.rationale: Self-contained scenario. No cross-scenario UI dependency. But creates another admin surface to maintain.

options.label: API-only, no admin UI (CLI + API for admin operations)
options.rationale: Fastest to ship. CLI already exists in authenticator. Admin operations via API/CLI only. UI can be added later.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: User data deletion is legally required in many jurisdictions and architecturally complex when data spans multiple scenarios. This needs to be designed upfront. Recommendation: Option B — soft delete with hard purge is the pragmatic balance.

options.label: Hard delete immediately (cascade across all tables)
options.rationale: Simplest implementation. Full compliance. Risk: accidental deletion is irreversible. Cascading deletes across scenarios require coordination.

options.label: Soft delete with 30-day grace period, then hard purge
options.rationale: Industry standard. Users can recover accounts. Background job handles final purge. More complex but safer.

options.label: Anonymize in place (null PII fields, keep record)
options.rationale: Preserves referential integrity and analytics. Technically compliant. But some jurisdictions may require full erasure.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.context: Scale affects architecture choices (caching strategy, pagination approach, search implementation). The Vrooli server currently runs locally with a small number of users, but scenarios may be deployed as SaaS. Recommendation: Option B covers most realistic deployments.

options.label: Under 100 users (local/personal use)
options.rationale: Simplest. No pagination needed. In-memory search is fine. Minimal caching.

options.label: 100–10,000 users (small-to-medium SaaS)
options.rationale: Needs cursor pagination, basic search indexing, Redis caching for hot profiles. Covers most realistic deployments.

options.label: 10,000+ users (enterprise scale)
options.rationale: Needs full-text search (possibly dedicated search service), aggressive caching, rate limiting, bulk operations API.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.text: scenario-authenticator already has comprehensive auth capabilities: user registration, login, JWT tokens, password reset, Redis sessions, PostgreSQL storage, OAuth2 (Google, GitHub), RBAC (admin/user roles), API keys, rate limiting, 2FA (TOTP), audit logging, and CLI user management commands. All P0 and P1 features are marked as verified. This is a strong foundation to build on.

The authenticator's P2 wishlist includes 'User impersonation for admins' and 'Passwordless login via magic links' — these could be absorbed into the user-mgmt scope if desired, providing a natural migration path for features that don't fit cleanly in auth.
